receipts and execution logs, plus trusted current source/run/attempt and explicit
successful native, producer and aggregate consumer job outcomes. It checks two
distinct complete executions and their exact disjoint union without comparing
its own Ubuntu platform/root to Darwin. Never upload consumer runtime binaries
or invent LCOV for uninstrumented tests.

Archive qualification must remove producer build outputs and inspect actual
application stack frame file:line evidence separately from panic-header source
locations. Successful binary execution alone does not prove diagnostics survived.
Darwin unpacked line tables depend on compiler objects that official archives do
not retain. The macOS profile generates only metadata-selected executable dSYM
bundles with Apple `dsymutil` and includes them through official Nextest archive
extras, keeping the line-table profile unchanged. Require the producer extraction
probe and every consumer to verify the actual expected symbol inventory and
bytes, since repository configuration can override lower-priority tool extras.
The archive/manifest hashes bind these symbols. Retain a missing-bundle negative
control in `scripts/ci/macos-remaining-cli.test.mjs`; do not archive the whole
compiler cache. Measure symbol generation, added bytes and complete hosted
compile/transfer/queue cost before claiming a speedup.

Cancel superseded verification for the same candidate when safe, with concurrency
groups that separate caller workflows, event streams and branches. Reusable Health
keeps a distinct prefix because GitHub exposes the caller workflow in its context;
PR/merge candidates cancel their superseded source. Push verification uses a unique
run ID in its concurrency group: disabling cancellation alone still permits a
newer pending run to replace an older pending run. Every main commit must retain
its complete verification for release consumers, while scheduled and manual
evidence streams remain isolated. Preserve
publication and release ordering. Inspect the configured queue mode and
cancellation semantics; do not assume workflow dispatch order is execution order.
Concurrency groups do not supply merge-candidate validation. Follow GitHub's
[concurrency semantics](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/control-workflow-concurrency)
and the project's [merge-check rules](testing-feedback-loop.md#merge-queues-and-required-merge-checks).

## Fix instability at the owning boundary

Classify a failure before changing its budget: product regression, fixture race,
resource exhaustion, dependency/service failure or unavailable infrastructure.
Retain the failing source and attempt, first error, relevant trace and measured
phase. A passing rerun is diagnostic information, not a root-cause explanation.
Playwright explicitly [classifies a retry pass as flaky](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries);
keep first-attempt and retry outcomes distinct.

Synchronize with observable readiness and the exact operation being tested.
Register observers before triggering transient events; correlate signals with
request identity, immutable control state and the lifetime of the actual task.
Historical logs or a previously authenticated request do not prove that a live
request has entered the required phase. Keep cancellation, task joining and
cleanup correct on success, failure and panic.
When key ordering determines the scenario, use deterministic noncolliding fixture
identities and check actual signed keys or cursors; random IDs can exercise only
the easier path. Preserve real signing, publication and receipt assertions.
Keep commit, completed publication and recipient installation distinct. A
post-timeout snapshot can block behind the publisher and cannot prove its state
existed before the cutoff; record phases at the actual work owner.
Use the owning register-before-check notification protocol for durable status;
polling an in-memory flag can still compete with the work that must publish it.
Match a fixture's executor to its requirement: preserve single-thread tests when
responsiveness is the subject, and keep independent protocol/persistence workers
for other production-runtime scenarios. Join admitted work before deleting data.
Classify fixture gates from the current decision owner's state, not a trace flag
that also describes another phase. Do not sample a later observer projection to
decide whether to capture a one-shot event; observe that evidence before releasing
the captured task and retain its exact operation and child identity.

Separate expensive fixture preparation from the operation's measured window when
preparation is outside the requirement. Continue using the real signing,
persistence, transport or UI owner when it is part of the assertion. Preserve
production deadlines and real lifecycle coverage where those are the subject of
the test; changing the clock or injecting state cannot silently remove them.
A held real socket still consumes its production timeout while a fixture waits.
Finish unrelated cold preparation before dispatching that read, using a scoped
owned barrier before I/O where necessary. Do not pause a post-send hook to conceal
the network timeout. Consolidate repeated readiness polls into that preparation
owner; retain exact live-task and measured-operation assertions at admission.

Batch unobserved durable fixture construction through an existing validated
transaction seam when individual commit boundaries are outside the requirement.
Retain every signed event, per-event validation and index update, a completed
durable commit before observation, exact corpus assertions and the original
measured operation. Never batch away the transaction boundaries under test.
Commit CLI fixture infrastructure to its private baseline before introducing the
intended source change; unrelated copied tools must not inflate changed-file
validation or consume the assertion's watchdog.

Lifecycle regressions should exercise the real supervisor and child processes
without making unrelated host tool startup part of their success condition.
When tool identity is outside the assertion, reuse the existing
[tool-version fixture](../scripts/diagnostics/test-fixtures/tool-versions.mjs)
and verify that its probes were actually consumed. Keep the real command,
failure, cancellation and receipt assertions and their existing watchdogs.
Compare nested budgets before adding an outer subprocess timeout: several valid
inner probes can exhaust it before the behavior under test starts. A passing PR
run cannot qualify an unbounded environmental dependency for later main runs.

Executable fixtures must own an independent copied image, not a hard link to
the running test harness. Assert file identity before launch. After verified
process retirement, use the shared bounded filesystem cleanup helper; persistent
locks must still fail. Keep the Windows held-image failure and release controls
in `release-reuse.test.mjs`; cleanup retries never retry the test assertion or
substitute for process retirement.

Git-path and mode controls should construct Git objects when the host cannot
represent the input faithfully. Assert the actual delta and mode before checking
rejection; an empty change rejected for another reason is not a valid negative
control. Keep these cases on every platform instead of skipping them.

Browser commands use the existing process owner with a deadline inside the total
job budget, reserving time for joined cleanup and evidence upload. Keep streamed
logs and append-only active/completed-case progress when final reports cannot be
written. Timeout or uncertain cleanup remains a failure. Preserve verified closure of owned work as a diagnostic separately from the
actual child outcome: Windows
intentionally terminates even an empty job to close descendant admission.
On POSIX, verify the framework's independently grouped web server as well as the
CLI group. Use its supported graceful interruption protocol; a missing teardown
acknowledgment means cleanup remains unverified. Bind lifecycle markers to the
current invocation so old evidence cannot prove a later process stopped.
Do not await output-pipe closure indefinitely after the command leader exits.
The existing process owner bounds draining after group retirement; a separately
grouped descendant retaining stdout or stderr must yield a failed structured
result with unverified cleanup and a quarantined lease. Closing owned read ends
does not prove the escaped process stopped. Keep real natural-exit, cancellation
and no-success-receipt controls rather than signalling unknown process groups.
Authorize PID cleanup only from a complete private acknowledgment, not a numeric
prefix in a stdout chunk. Stream reads do not preserve message boundaries; a
failed readiness publication must retire the child through its creation owner.
Actual CLI regression fixtures need private output directories as well as private
source directories; parallel Playwright commands otherwise delete one another's
traces and manufacture failures. Missing hosted logs do not identify a slow case.
Local-only evidence fixtures must explicitly isolate and restore inherited CI
flags, and separately assert that real CI cannot reuse local acceptance evidence.
Health captures its absolute budget before setup and uses the existing stage
owner to stop diagnostics before the job watchdog. Preserve its structured result,
execution log and bounded Node lifecycle records, including the active file/case,
through the always-upload path. Prove interruption and joined cleanup with a real
parked command. Missing hosted logs require better evidence, not a guessed fix.
Cancellation during preparation still needs a failed structured result. Only the
command owner can attest that admission never happened; failures after that
boundary must retain uncertain cleanup rather than manufacture a no-work result.

The [fixture timing guidance](testing-feedback-loop.md#cold-fixture-preparation-versus-measured-progress)
owns concrete examples and permitted boundaries.

Prefer bounded condition waits and meaningful failure diagnostics. Browser
actions should use [Playwright actionability and retrying assertions](https://playwright.dev/docs/actionability)
where applicable; application readiness may still need its own signal. Arbitrary
sleeps, broader timeouts, blanket retries and weaker assertions need evidence;
they are not default repairs for an unexplained failure. If a narrowly scoped
infrastructure retry is justified, keep its limit, original failure and outcomes
visible, and ensure repeating the operation is safe. Test retries still obey the
owning suite policy.

Keep each observation inside a polling assertion nonwaiting when the assertion
already owns readiness. A locator operation can wait for a virtualized row and
consume the entire outer budget without producing one geometry sample. Inspect
the trace to distinguish missing samples from unequal values; use one browser-side
DOM snapshot for transient geometry, treating an absent row as pending. Preserve
exact geometry and cache assertions, and exercise the absent-row control rather
than extending the deadline. The media-scroll remount regression owns this case.

For a reproducible race or timeout fix, use a regression or negative control that
fails for the original mechanism and passes with the repair. Confirm that the
intended case actually ran. Preserve existing coverage while investigating; any
temporary quarantine needs an explicit owner, reason, tracking issue and removal
condition under the existing gate policy.

## Reject incomplete discovery and generated-policy drift

Successful test execution requires successful, complete input discovery.
`scripts/ci/fuzz-targets.py` compares the discovered cargo-fuzz list with the actual
manifest-owned target inventory before running anything. Failed enumeration, an
empty list, duplicates, omissions or unknown targets fail the job, as do individual
target failures. Keep this assertion at the execution owner; shell loop command
substitution alone does not propagate discovery failure under `set -e`.

`scripts/ci/glib-migration.py` evaluates every resolved glib branch, rather than
treating a newer parallel branch as proof that an older stack was removed. Its
migration claim conservatively requires stable 0.20 or newer throughout; absent
glib and mixed old/new trees do not establish migration. The
[RustSec advisory](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2024-0429.html) owns the
security version ranges; the watcher retains native build/test and reviewed-PR
requirements before changing dependencies.

Generated native input probes share one accepted-key/extended-flag metadata owner
between WebDriver mapping and emitted C# policy. Regressions must check that every
emitted key is accepted with the correct flags and unsupported keys remain
rejected, rather than only matching the generated call text. Ownership checks and
real desktop acceptance remain separate from generator/compilation checks.

## Review the change and prevent renewed drift

Follow the existing validation stages; do not invent a parallel completion
process. For changes affecting CI behavior or recurring cost, include the
following in the normal [alignment review](maintenance-checklist.md#review-and-follow-up-procedure):

- The acceptance boundary and retained owner, including consumers affected by
  deletion, merging, selection or schedule changes.
- The measured bottleneck, comparable before/after scope and remaining unknowns;
  distinguish observed latency, resource cost and reliability.
- Executed validation and source identity, with inventory/provenance checks or
  regression controls appropriate to the changed mechanism.
- Remaining hosted, cross-platform, native or release evidence and the owner of
  any follow-up. Do not claim candidate acceptance from local or older results.

Workflow, runner and tool upgrades can change CLI semantics, report formats,
selectors and archive compatibility. Validate affected real tool invocations and
failure paths through the existing diagnostic owners; YAML parsing or unit mocks
alone do not establish the behavior of the installed tool.

Consolidate frontend unit execution through the complete Linux coverage owner
when the ordinary and coverage commands select the same inventory and platform
branches use explicit mocks. Verify that inventory with the actual runner before
removing duplicate OS executions. Retain real browser/native matrices and native
diagnostic fixtures; mocked platform branches do not supply those contracts.
Keep Node/filesystem portability requirements in their owning diagnostics rather
than duplicating the entire frontend unit suite incidentally.

Keep platform-exclusive probes in the required native producer that can execute
them. Universal local selections must not include a file whose entire suite is
skipped on other hosts; preserve the nonempty-test guard and explicit native
escalation instead. Keep workflow wiring assertions in the cheap CI policy
owner, separate from the underlying tool's filesystem/compiler regressions.

After pushing, observe the actual hosted candidate until the relevant jobs finish.
Compare before and after setup time, test time, required-check latency and runner
minutes with sample sizes and cache conditions. Inspect first failures and queue
changes, then make another measured pass when evidence identifies remaining waste.
A pushed branch, a local green subset, or a faster isolated step does not establish
an end-to-end speedup. Keep the candidate reviewable and continue in a clean
worktree when unrelated local edits prevent publication; do not discard those
edits or treat them as a reason to stop the optimization.

Revisit timing and failure evidence when a gate becomes slower, starts rerunning,
gains another platform/dependency, or repeatedly exceeds its expected budget.
During existing maintenance reviews, inspect slow cases, duplicated setup,
shard imbalance, cache churn and abandoned temporary exceptions. Retire obsolete
work with its consumers and selectors rather than accumulating permanent layers.

Keep this review proportional: a documentation-only change needs applicable
formatting, links and structural checks, not a new build benchmark. Rules should
be enforceable through existing contracts and diagnostics where practical;
adding this guide does not create a scheduled job or another required check.

Query can be a natural-language question OR a bag of symbol/file names. Usually the ONLY call you need — more accurate context, in far fewer tokens and round-trips than a search/Read/Grep loop.

# Codegraph — available (per-project; pass projectPath)

Codegraph is a SQLite knowledge graph of a codebase's symbols, edges, and
files: one `codegraph_explore` call returns the verbatim, line-numbered source
of the relevant symbols PLUS the call paths between them and a blast-radius
summary — replacing a grep + Read loop with one round-trip.

This server started somewhere with no `.codegraph/` of its own, so there is no
default project — but the tools are available and work **per project**:

- To query a project that HAS a `.codegraph/` index (e.g. a service inside a
  monorepo, or a second repo), pass its path as `projectPath` to
  `codegraph_explore` (and any other codegraph tool). Codegraph resolves the
  nearest `.codegraph/` at or above that path and answers from it — for as many
  projects as you like in one session.
- For a project with no `.codegraph/`, use your built-in tools (Read/Grep/Glob)
  for that project. Indexing is the user's decision — don't run it yourself, but
  if it comes up they can run `codegraph init` in a project to enable codegraph
  there (a new index is picked up live, no restart).

exec tool declaration:
```ts
declare const tools: { mcp__codegraph__codegraph_explore(args: {
  // Maximum number of files to include source code from (default: 12)
  maxFiles?: number;
  // Absolute path to the project to query (or any directory inside it) — codegraph uses the nearest .codegraph/ index at or above that path. Omit to use this session's default project. Pass it to query a second codebase, or when the server root has no index of its own (e.g. a monorepo where only sub-projects are indexed, so there is no default project).
  projectPath: string;
  // Symbol names, file names, or short code terms to explore (e.g., "AuthService loginUser session-manager", "GraphTraverser BFS impact traversal.ts"). For a flow question, name the symbols spanning the flow (e.g. "mutateElement renderScene"). A natural-language question works too — no prior codegraph_search needed.
  query: string;
}): Promise<CallToolResult>; };
```"}]

name: CI

on:
  merge_group:
    types: [checks_requested]
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * 1" # Preserve the former weekly full-health Rust run.
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      diagnostic_timing:
        description: Full-workspace test-only delivery phase timings
        type: boolean
        default: false

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.event_name }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}-${{ github.event_name == 'push' && github.run_id || 'candidate' }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' || github.event_name == 'merge_group' }}

# Read-only: every job just checks out and runs tooling — nothing writes back.
permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  CARGO_TERM_COLOR: always
  # Keep stack file/line diagnostics without generating type/variable debug data.
  CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG: line-tables-only
  CARGO_PROFILE_TEST_DEBUG: line-tables-only
  MESH_TALK_TEST_TIMING: ${{ inputs.diagnostic_timing && '1' || '0' }}

jobs:
  scope:
    uses: ./.github/workflows/ci-scope.yml

  checks:
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    needs: [scope]
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      # Windows uses the reusable single-build archive workflow below. Linux
      # and macOS retain complete workspace tests; macOS instruments Host only.
      # Keep compute-heavy protocol tests on Apple Silicon. Desktop browser
      # admission separately waits for Health/WebKit and bounds its fan-out.
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ needs.scope.outputs.full == 'true' && matrix.os || 'ubuntu-latest' }}
    timeout-minutes: 90
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          fetch-depth: 2
      - id: scope
        uses: ./.github/actions/ci-scope
        with:
          full: ${{ needs.scope.outputs.full }}
          upstream_result: ${{ needs.scope.result }}
      - name: Report documentation-only coverage through Codecov
        if: steps.scope.outputs.full == 'false' && matrix.os == 'ubuntu-latest'
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@303a32d7a59b442fa8d48b6a1cc6825c09c847a5 # v7.1.1
        with:
          version: v11.3.2

          fail_ci_if_error: true
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        if: ${{ steps.scope.outputs.full == 'true' }}
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm
          cache-dependency-path: frontend/package-lock.json

      - name: Prepare hosted Linux build storage
        if: ${{ steps.scope.outputs.full == 'true' && (runner.os == 'Linux') }}
        id: runner_storage
        shell: bash
        run: sudo --preserve-env=GITHUB_ACTIONS,RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT,RUNNER_OS "$(command -v node)" scripts/ci/runner-storage.mjs --prepare | tee "$RUNNER_TEMP/runner-storage.json"

      - name: Preserve runner storage measurements
        if: ${{ steps.scope.outputs.full == 'true' && (always() && steps.runner_storage.outcome == 'success') }}
        continue-on-error: true
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: runner-storage-${{ github.job }}-${{ strategy.job-index || 0 }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}
          path: ${{ runner.temp }}/runner-storage.json
          if-no-files-found: error
          retention-days: 14

      - name: Prepare Ubuntu archive source
        if: ${{ steps.scope.outputs.full == 'true' && (runner.os == 'Linux') }}
        shell: bash
        run: sudo --preserve-env=GITHUB_ACTIONS,RUNNER_ENVIRONMENT,RUNNER_OS "$(command -v node)" scripts/ci/ubuntu-apt-source.mjs

      - name: Install Tauri system dependencies (Linux)
        if: ${{ steps.scope.outputs.full == 'true' && (matrix.os == 'ubuntu-latest') }}

          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y \
            libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev \
            libgtk-3-dev \

**Smallest DAG**

1. Linux native checks: frontend/standards, Clippy, production workspace build, doctests, existing compiler/crash fixtures.

Uploading from the middle of the producer cannot unblock consumers. Native checks must be independent of the producer, and ignored execution must be a separate consumer job.

- `LARGE_FOLDER_SCENARIO` at line 17 owns large-folder exact selection.
- Bridge currently runs every ignored case in `bridge_cross_lan`: four cases. Derive that selection from the archived target inventory; do not introduce another hand-maintained name list.
- Keep `verifyPartition` unchanged: it explicitly forbids ignored execution. Add a separate strict ignored-selection validator.

Use the actual archive-extracted libtest executable, selected from verified binary metadata, through the existing `runCargo(..., { command })` seam. Preserve `evaluateBackendSuites`, redacted log digests, report shape, original error precedence, cancellation/cleanup behavior and all actual captured fixture output. Keep stdout distinct from stderr; existing tests explicitly reject merged or truncated machine evidence.

**Path and runtime constraints**

The current archive helper hardcodes workspace `target` in identity, layout, extraction, profile-path validation and metadata locations. Old Linux coverage naturally uses `target/llvm-cov-target`. Add a profile-owned absolute target directory and thread it through those existing operations rather than silently migrating Linux cache cohorts.

`CARGO_BIN_EXE_mesh-talk-node` is compiled into CLI fixtures, including Bridge. Consumers must restore the executable to that original absolute path. Nextest target remapping alone cannot rewrite it. Qualify extraction/rename using the actual pinned archive tool and a tiny fixture launching its embedded CLI after producer outputs are removed.

Pin Linux producer/consumers to `ubuntu-24.04`; bind architecture, compiler, coverage tool, Cargo configuration, profile, exact target/root, source/run/attempt, archive/config/inventory digests and runtime ABI cohort. Consumers need Tauri runtime libraries for Host execution; qualify an explicit runtime package set using real archived Host execution and dependency inspection. Do not assume compile headers alone define runtime compatibility. Retain Ubuntu APT/storage owners.

Linux ELF line tables should require no Darwin dSYM extras, but qualify actual application stack file:line after deleting producer outputs.

**Coverage and trust**

Require trusted producer manifest/archive hashes for Linux instrumented consumers as well as current source/run/attempt and successful upstream outcomes. Each default shard and ignored consumer exports coverage from its own fresh execution. Their LCOV union is legitimate; never combine an interim report with its later superset. Validate nonempty measured Host/Core sources and hashes, exact default partition union, exact ignored selections and complete successful executions. Preserve all original checks and ignored/doctest policies.

**Qualification controls**

Use tiny actual-tool fixtures for:

- Default + ignored coverage contributing distinct functions.
- Embedded CLI path surviving archive-only execution.
- Omitted/duplicate/default-ignored leakage and unexpected ignored selection.
- Exact large-folder selection excluding a similarly named panic case.
- Corrupt archive/manifest, source/attempt/runtime/profile/path drift.
- Real failure, timeout, cancellation, truncated stdout and uncertain cleanup.
- Archive-only Host execution with installed Linux runtime libraries.
- ELF stack file:line without producer build outputs.

**Expected benefit and cost**

Known instrumented compilation totals approximately 12m21s. Two shards could reduce the current roughly 16-minute default execution tail, while the ignored consumer’s approximately 8m12s runs concurrently. A warm idealized archive path is therefore around 20–23 minutes plus setup, archive transfer, reporting and queueing. Hash imbalance and cold dependencies remain unknown; this is not evidence of a 30-minute complete DAG.

This adds three Linux execution consumers while avoiding their Rust caches/builds. Keep the existing canonical native cache writer unless measured cohort/cache compatibility justifies a deliberate budgeted change; do not add competing writers or unqualified cache rotation. Assess global 20-job/Mac five-job admission against the full hosted DAG, including simultaneous Windows eight-way and macOS two-way phases.

---
name: test-driven-development
description: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
---

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

---

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency.

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence ≠ evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter ≠ compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion ≠ excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
✅ [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
❌ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
✅ Write → Run (pass) → Revert fix → Run (MUST FAIL) → Restore → Run (pass)
❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
❌ Trust agent report
```

## Why This Matters

From 24 failure memories:
- your human partner said "I don't believe you" - trust broken
- Undefined functions shipped - would crash
- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features
- Time wasted on false completion → redirect → rework
- Violates: "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced."

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

## The Bottom Line

**No shortcuts for verification.**

Run the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.

This is non-negotiable.

name: brainstorming
description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
---

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

# Test-Driven Development (TDD)

## Overview

Write the test first. Watch it fail. Write minimal code to pass.

**Core principle:** If you didn't watch the test fail, you don't know if it tests the right thing.

**Violating the letter of the rules is violating the spirit of the rules.**

## When to Use

**Always:**
- New features
- Bug fixes
- Refactoring
- Behavior changes

**Exceptions (ask your human partner):**
- Throwaway prototypes
- Generated code
- Configuration files

Thinking "skip TDD just this once"? Stop. That's rationalization.

## The Iron Law

```
NO PRODUCTION CODE WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

Write code before the test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete

Implement fresh from tests. Period.

## Red-Green-Refactor

```dot
digraph tdd_cycle {
    rankdir=LR;
    red [label="RED\nWrite failing test", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ffcccc"];
    verify_red [label="Verify fails\ncorrectly", shape=diamond];
    green [label="GREEN\nMinimal code", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccffcc"];
    verify_green [label="Verify passes\nAll green", shape=diamond];
    refactor [label="REFACTOR\nClean up", shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor="#ccccff"];
    next [label="Next", shape=ellipse];

    red -> verify_red;
    verify_red -> green [label="yes"];
    verify_red -> red [label="wrong\nfailure"];
    green -> verify_green;
    verify_green -> refactor [label="yes"];
    verify_green -> green [label="no"];
    refactor -> verify_green [label="stay\ngreen"];
    verify_green -> next;
    next -> red;
}
```

### RED - Write Failing Test

Write one minimal test showing what should happen.

<Good>
```typescript
test('retries failed operations 3 times', async () => {
  let attempts = 0;
  const operation = () => {
    attempts++;
    if (attempts < 3) throw new Error('fail');
    return 'success';
  };

  const result = await retryOperation(operation);

  expect(result).toBe('success');
  expect(attempts).toBe(3);
});
```
Clear name, tests real behavior, one thing
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
test('retry works', async () => {
  const mock = jest.fn()
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error())
    .mockResolvedValueOnce('success');
  await retryOperation(mock);
  expect(mock).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(3);
});
```
Vague name, tests mock not code
</Bad>

**Requirements:**
- One behavior
- Clear name
- Real code (no mocks unless unavoidable)

### Verify RED - Watch It Fail

**MANDATORY. Never skip.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test fails (not errors)
- Failure message is expected
- Fails because feature missing (not typos)

**Test passes?** You're testing existing behavior. Fix test.

**Test errors?** Fix error, re-run until it fails correctly.

### GREEN - Minimal Code

Write simplest code to pass the test.

<Good>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(fn: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (e) {
      if (i === 2) throw e;
    }
  }
  throw new Error('unreachable');
}
```
Just enough to pass
</Good>

<Bad>
```typescript
async function retryOperation<T>(
  fn: () => Promise<T>,
  options?: {
    maxRetries?: number;
    backoff?: 'linear' | 'exponential';
    onRetry?: (attempt: number) => void;
  }
): Promise<T> {
  // YAGNI
}
```
Over-engineered
</Bad>

Don't add features, refactor other code, or "improve" beyond the test.

### Verify GREEN - Watch It Pass

**MANDATORY.**

```bash
npm test path/to/test.test.ts
```

Confirm:
- Test passes
- Other tests still pass
- Output pristine (no errors, warnings)

**Test fails?** Fix code, not test.

**Other tests fail?** Fix now.

### REFACTOR - Clean Up

After green only:
- Remove duplication
- Improve names
- Extract helpers

Keep tests green. Don't add behavior.

### Repeat

Next failing test for next feature.

## Good Tests

| Quality | Good | Bad |
|---------|------|-----|
| **Minimal** | One thing. "and" in name? Split it. | `test('validates email and domain and whitespace')` |
| **Clear** | Name describes behavior | `test('test1')` |
| **Shows intent** | Demonstrates desired API | Obscures what code should do |

## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.

**"Tests after achieve the same goals - it's spirit not ritual"**

No. Tests-after answer "What does this do?" Tests-first answer "What should this do?"

Tests-after are biased by your implementation. You test what you built, not what's required. You verify remembered edge cases, not discovered ones.

Tests-first force edge case discovery before implementing. Tests-after verify you remembered everything (you didn't).

30 minutes of tests after ≠ TDD. You get coverage, lose proof tests work.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
| "Already manually tested" | Ad-hoc ≠ systematic. No record, can't re-run. |
| "Deleting X hours is wasteful" | Sunk cost fallacy. Keeping unverified code is technical debt. |
| "Keep as reference, write tests first" | You'll adapt it. That's testing after. Delete means delete. |
| "Need to explore first" | Fine. Throw away exploration, start with TDD. |
| "Test hard = design unclear" | Listen to test. Hard to test = hard to use. |
| "TDD will slow me down" | TDD faster than debugging. Pragmatic = test-first. |
| "Manual test faster" | Manual doesn't prove edge cases. You'll re-test every change. |
| "Existing code has no tests" | You're improving it. Add tests for existing code. |

## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- Test after implementation
- Test passes immediately
- Can't explain why test failed
- Tests added "later"
- Rationalizing "just this once"
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "Keep as reference" or "adapt existing code"
- "Already spent X hours, deleting is wasteful"
- "TDD is dogmatic, I'm being pragmatic"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**

## Example: Bug Fix

**Bug:** Empty email accepted

**RED**
```typescript
test('rejects empty email', async () => {
  const result = await submitForm({ email: '' });
  expect(result.error).toBe('Email required');
});
```

**Verify RED**
```bash
$ npm test
FAIL: expected 'Email required', got undefined
```

**GREEN**
```typescript
function submitForm(data: FormData) {
  if (!data.email?.trim()) {
    return { error: 'Email required' };
  }
  // ...
}
```

**Verify GREEN**
```bash
$ npm test
PASS
```

**REFACTOR**
Extract validation for multiple fields if needed.

## Verification Checklist

Before marking work complete:

- [ ] Every new function/method has a test
- [ ] Watched each test fail before implementing
- [ ] Each test failed for expected reason (feature missing, not typo)
- [ ] Wrote minimal code to pass each test
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Output pristine (no errors, warnings)
- [ ] Tests use real code (mocks only if unavoidable)
- [ ] Edge cases and errors covered

Can't check all boxes? You skipped TDD. Start over.

## When Stuck

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| Don't know how to test | Write wished-for API. Write assertion first. Ask your human partner. |
| Test too complicated | Design too complicated. Simplify interface. |
| Must mock everything | Code too coupled. Use dependency injection. |
| Test setup huge | Extract helpers. Still complex? Simplify design. |

## Debugging Integration

Bug found? Write failing test reproducing it. Follow TDD cycle. Test proves fix and prevents regression.

Never fix bugs without a test.

## Testing Anti-Patterns

When adding mocks or test utilities, read @testing-anti-patterns.md to avoid common pitfalls:
- Testing mock behavior instead of real behavior
- Adding test-only methods to production classes
- Mocking without understanding dependencies

## Final Rule

```
Production code → test exists and failed first
Otherwise → not TDD
```

No exceptions without your human partner's permission.

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency.

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verificatio…176 tokens truncated…ore → Run (pass)
❌ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
✅ [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
❌ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
✅ Re-read plan → Create checklist → Verify each → Report gaps or completion
❌ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
✅ Agent reports success → Check VCS diff → Verify changes → Report actual state
❌ Trust agent report
```

## Why This Matters

From 24 failure memories:
- your human partner said "I don't believe you" - trust broken
- Undefined functions shipped - would crash
- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features
- Time wasted on false completion → redirect → rework
- Violates: "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced."

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

## The Bottom Line

**No shortcuts for verification.**

Run the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.

This is non-negotiable.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

  const observed = listings.map(inventory);
  verifyPartition(observed[0], observed.slice(1), profile.partitions.length);
  assert.deepEqual(
    observed,
    expected,
    "Consumer partition differs from producer inventory",
  );
  writeJson(path.join(output, "selected-inventory.json"), observed[shard]);
  const started = performance.now();
  const events = await command(
    [
      "nextest",
      "run",
      ...nextestArgs,
      ...reuse,
      "--partition",
      `hash:${shard}/${profile.partitions.length}`,
      "--test-threads",
      String(profile.testThreads),
      "--retries",
      "0",
      profile.instrumented ? consumerFailurePolicy() : "--no-fail-fast",
      "--no-tests",
      "fail",
      ...(process.env.MESH_TALK_TEST_TIMING === "1"
        ? ["--success-output", "final"]
        : []),
      "--message-format",
      "libtest-json-plus",
      "--message-format-version",
      "0.1",
    ],
    {
      env: {
        ...process.env,
        CARGO_NET_OFFLINE: "true",
        RUST_TEST_THREADS: String(profile.testThreads),
        NEXTEST_EXPERIMENTAL_LIBTEST_JSON: "1",
      },
      ...evidence("execution"),
      liveStdout: true,
    },
  );
  verifyExecution(events, observed[shard]);
  let coverageEvidence = {};
  if (profile.instrumented) {
    const coverageFile = path.join(output, "coverage.lcov");
    await command(
      ["llvm-cov", "report", "--lcov", "--output-path", coverageFile],
      {
        env: { ...process.env, CARGO_NET_OFFLINE: "true" },
        ...evidence("coverage"),
      },
    );
    const coverage = validateLcov(readFileSync(coverageFile, "utf8"));
    coverageEvidence = {
      coverageSha256: await fileHash(coverageFile),
      coverage,
    };
  }
  verifyIdentity(
    manifest.identity,
    await identity((phase) => evidence(`final-${phase}`), profile),
  );
  writeJson(path.join(output, "receipt.json"), {
    schema: 1,
    sourceSha: manifest.identity.sourceSha,
    runId: manifest.identity.runId,
    runAttempt: manifest.identity.runAttempt,
    shard,
    archiveSha256: manifest.archiveSha256,
    manifestSha256: await fileHash(path.join(directory, "manifest.json")),
    ...coverageEvidence,
    ...(!profile.instrumented
      ? {
          identity: manifest.identity,
          featureResolutionSha256: manifest.featureResolutionSha256,
          inventoryFiles: manifest.inventoryFiles,
          selectedInventorySha256: await fileHash(
            path.join(output, "selected-inventory.json"),
          ),
        }
      : {}),
    executionSha256: await fileHash(path.join(output, "execution.jsonl")),
    seconds: (performance.now() - started) / 1000,
    executedTests: observed[shard].filter((row) => row.selected).length,
    totalTests: observed[0].length,
  });
  console.log(
    `Shard ${shard}/${profile.partitions.length} passed exact inventory${profile.instrumented ? " and coverage" : ""} validation.`,
  );
}

// Pure cross-platform collection: producer job outputs are authority, never this
// collector's platform/root or an artifact's self-reported checksum.
export async function collectMacRemaining(directory, outputs, trusted) {
  requireDigest(trusted?.manifestSha256);
  requireDigest(trusted?.archiveSha256);
  assert.deepEqual(
    trusted.jobResults,
    { native: "success", producer: "success", consumers: "success" },
    "All native archive job results must be success",
  );
  assert.match(
    trusted.sourceSha ?? "",
    /^[a-f0-9]{40}$/u,
    "Expected source SHA required",
  );
  assert.match(trusted.runId ?? "", /^[1-9]\d*$/u, "Expected run ID required");
  assert.match(
    trusted.runAttempt ?? "",
    /^[1-9]\d*$/u,
    "Expected attempt required",
  );
  assert.equal(
    await fileHash(path.join(directory, "manifest.json")),
    trusted.manifestSha256,
    "Trusted manifest digest mismatch",
  );
  const manifest = readJson(path.join(directory, "manifest.json"));
  const profile = archiveProfile("macos-remaining");
  assert.equal(manifest.schema, 1, "Unsupported archive manifest");
  assert.equal(
    manifest.identity.archiveProfile,
    profile.name,
    "Wrong archive profile",
  );
  assert.equal(manifest.identity.platform, "darwin", "Wrong producer platform");
  for (const key of ["sourceSha", "runId", "runAttempt"])
    assert.equal(manifest.identity[key], trusted[key], `Stale producer ${key}`);
  assert.equal(
    manifest.archiveSha256,
    trusted.archiveSha256,
    "Trusted archive digest mismatch",
  );
  assert.equal(
    digest(
      canonical(readJson(path.join(directory, "feature-resolution.json"))),
    ),
    manifest.featureResolutionSha256,
    "Producer feature resolution digest mismatch",
  );
  assert.deepEqual(
    manifest.scheduling,
    scheduling(profile),
    "Wrong archive scheduling",
  );
  const expected = [];
  assert.deepEqual(
    Object.keys(manifest.inventoryFiles).sort(),
    ["inventory-0.json", "inventory-1.json", "inventory-2.json"],
    "Unexpected inventory files",
  );
  for (let index = 0; index <= 2; index++) {
    const name = `inventory-${index}.json`;
    assert.equal(
      await fileHash(path.join(directory, name)),
      manifest.inventoryFiles[name],
      "Producer inventory digest mismatch",
    );
    expected.push(readJson(path.join(directory, name)));
  }
  verifyPartition(expected[0], expected.slice(1), 2);
  assert.equal(
    manifest.testCount,
    expected[0].length,
    "Producer total test count mismatch",
  );
  assert.equal(
    manifest.runnableCount,
    expected[0].filter((row) => row.selected).length,
    "Producer runnable count mismatch",
  );
  assert.equal(outputs.length, 2, "Exactly two consumer receipts required");
  const seen = new Set();
  for (const output of outputs) {
    const receipt = readJson(path.join(output, "receipt.json"));
    assert.equal(receipt.schema, 1, "Unsupported consumer receipt");
    assert.ok(
      profile.partitions.includes(receipt.shard) && !seen.has(receipt.shard),
      "Missing or duplicate consumer shard",
    );
    seen.add(receipt.shard);
    assert.ok(
      !("coverage" in receipt) && !("coverageSha256" in receipt),
      "Uninstrumented receipt cannot claim coverage",
    );
    verifyIdentity(manifest.identity, receipt.identity);
    for (const key of ["sourceSha", "runId", "runAttempt"])
      assert.equal(receipt[key], trusted[key], `Stale receipt ${key}`);
    assert.equal(
      receipt.archiveSha256,
      trusted.archiveSha256,
      "Receipt archive digest mismatch",
    );
    assert.equal(
      receipt.manifestSha256,
      trusted.manifestSha256,
      "Receipt manifest digest mismatch",
    );
    assert.equal(
      receipt.featureResolutionSha256,
      manifest.featureResolutionSha256,
      "Receipt feature graph differs",
    );
    assert.deepEqual(
      receipt.inventoryFiles,
      manifest.inventoryFiles,
      "Receipt inventories differ",
    );
    const selectedFile = path.join(output, "selected-inventory.json");
    assert.equal(
      await fileHash(selectedFile),
      receipt.selectedInventorySha256,
      "Selected inventory digest mismatch",
    );
    const selected = readJson(selectedFile);
    assert.deepEqual(
      selected,
      expected[receipt.shard],
      "Selected partition differs",
    );
    assert.equal(
      receipt.executedTests,
      selected.filter((row) => row.selected).length,
      "Execution count differs",
    );
    assert.equal(
      receipt.totalTests,
      expected[0].length,
      "Total inventory count differs",
    );
    assert.ok(
      Number.isFinite(receipt.seconds) && receipt.seconds >= 0,
      "Invalid execution duration",
    );
    const execution = path.join(output, "execution.jsonl");
    assert.equal(
      await fileHash(execution),
      receipt.executionSha256,
      "execution digest mismatch",
    );
    verifyExecution(readFileSync(execution, "utf8"), selected);
  }
  return {
    sourceSha: trusted.sourceSha,
    runId: trusted.runId,
    runAttempt: trusted.runAttempt,
    archiveSha256: trusted.archiveSha256,
    manifestSha256: trusted.manifestSha256,
    executedTests: manifest.runnableCount,
  };
}
function requireDigest(value) {
  assert.match(value ?? "", /^[a-f0-9]{64}$/u, "Trusted digest required");
}

async function main(args) {
  const [mode, ...values] = args;
  if (mode === "produce" && values.length === 1)
    await produce(path.resolve(values[0]));
  else if (mode === "consume" && values.length === 3)
    await consume(
      Number(values[0]),
      path.resolve(values[1]),
      path.resolve(values[2]),
    );
  else if (
    mode === "produce-macos-remaining" &&
    (values.length === 1 ||
      (values.length === 2 && values[1] === "--github-output"))
  ) {
    const result = await produce(path.resolve(values[0]), {
      profile: "macos-remaining",
    });
    if (values.length === 2) {
      assert.ok(
        process.env.GITHUB_OUTPUT,
        "GITHUB_OUTPUT is required for explicit export",
      );
      for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(result)) {
        assert.match(value ?? "", /^[a-zA-Z0-9.+-]+$/u, "Invalid job output");
        appendFileSync(process.env.GITHUB_OUTPUT, `${key}=${value}\n`);
      }
    }
  } else if (mode === "consume-macos-remaining" && values.length === 5) {
    await consume(
      Number(values[0]),
      path.resolve(values[1]),
      path.resolve(values[2]),
      {
        profile: "macos-remaining",
        manifestSha256: values[3],
        archiveSha256: values[4],
      },
    );
  } else if (mode === "collect-macos-remaining" && values.length === 5) {
    const result = await collectMacRemaining(
      path.resolve(values[0]),
      values.slice(1, 3).map((value) => path.resolve(value)),
      {
        manifestSha256: values[3],
        archiveSha256: values[4],
        sourceSha: process.env.GITHUB_SHA,
        runId: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ID,
        runAttempt: process.env.GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT,
        jobResults: {
          native: process.env.MESH_MACOS_NATIVE_RESULT,
          producer: process.env.MESH_MACOS_PRODUCER_RESULT,
          consumers: process.env.MESH_MACOS_CONSUMERS_RESULT,
        },
      },
    );
    console.log(JSON.stringify(result));
  } else
    throw new Error(
      "Usage: windows-coverage.mjs produce ARTIFACT_DIR | consume SHARD ARTIFACT_DIR OUTPUT_DIR | produce-macos-remaining ARTIFACT_DIR [--github-output] | consume-macos-remaining SHARD ARTIFACT_DIR OUTPUT_DIR MANIFEST_SHA256 ARCHIVE_SHA256 | collect-macos-remaining METADATA_DIR RESULT_1_DIR RESULT_2_DIR MANIFEST_SHA256 ARCHIVE_SHA256",
    );
}
if (
  process.argv[1] &&
  path.resolve(process.argv[1]) === fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)
)
  main(process.argv.slice(2)).catch((error) => {
    console.error(error.message);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  });
"}
